articles.title: Iran claims three tankers hit naval mines near Hormuz, warns ships against entering restricted zone
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Three oil tankers caught fire after reportedly striking naval mines in and around the Strait of Hormuz, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Three oil tankers caught fire after reportedly striking naval mines in and around the Strait of Hormuz, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy and Armed Forces Navy claimed on Saturday, warning other vessels against entering restricted maritime areas.According to Iranian state broadcaster Islamic Republic of Iran Broadcasting (IRIB), the IRGC Navy said two tankers attempting to cross the strategically important waterway without authorisation exploded and caught fire after hitting naval mines. The vessels were allegedly operating with their navigation and automatic identification systems switched off."An hour ago, two offending oil tankers, which were secretly attempting to transit the unauthorised Strait of Hormuz with their navigation and automatic identification systems turned off, exploded and caught fire after hitting naval mines," the statement said, as reported by IRIB.The IRGC Navy also claimed that two other tankers attempting to cross the strait turned back after receiving warnings from its Naval Traffic Control Centre."After the explosion of these two tankers, two other tankers that were attempting to secretly pass through the Strait of Hormuz heeded warnings from the IRGC's Naval Traffic Control Center and returned to the waters of the Persian Gulf," the statement added.Another tanker reported on fire east of Strait of HormuzIn a separate statement, Iran's Armed Forces Navy reported that another oil tanker had caught fire after striking a naval mine east of the Strait of Hormuz.According to the Navy's Public Relations department, the vessel had entered what it described as an unsafe and prohibited maritime zone despite previous warnings. It also alleged that the tanker had switched off its tracking and identification systems."This morning, an oil tanker that had been operating in the unsafe and prohibited area east of the Strait of Hormuz, ignoring previous warnings and turning off its tracking and identification systems, caught fire and stopped after hitting a naval mine," the statement said.The Navy warned that other vessels entering the restricted zone could face similar consequences."Without a doubt, any offending tanker that travels in the restricted area east of the Strait of Hormuz will be set on fire by hitting naval mines," it said.The statement also criticised tanker owners for sending their vessels into the restricted area, accusing them of relying on assurances from US President Donald Trump."It is unfortunate that tanker owners, without learning from the fate of other offending vessels, trusting the nonsense of the criminal US president, are sending their capital into the mine war and throwing it into the fire," the statement added.Strait of Hormuz emerges as flashpoint amid regional tensionsThe latest claims come amid escalating tensions involving Iran, the United States and Israel, with the Strait of Hormuz emerging as a key flashpoint in the West Asia conflict.The waterway is a critical route for global energy supplies, connecting the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea. Any disruption to shipping through the strait could affect international oil transportation and energy markets.Iranian authorities have repeatedly warned vessels against entering areas they have designated as restricted maritime zones. However, the latest claims of tanker fires and mine strikes have not been independently verified.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: A Chicago photographer spent $220 on two paintings at a Salvation Army thrift store in 2016; experts confirmed they were rare Warner Sallman originals, and a Colorado author bought them for $135,000 two years later
articles.summary: In 2016, Chicago photographer Paul Beaty walked into a Salvation Army thrift store with $300 in his pocket and left with two artworks priced at $125 each.
articles.body: In 2016, Chicago photographer Paul Beaty walked into a Salvation Army thrift store with $300 in his pocket and left with two artworks priced at $125 each. After negotiating the price down, he paid $220 in total for what turned out to be rare original works by Warner Sallman, the Chicago artist behind the widely reproduced 1940 painting Head of Christ. Two years later, Beaty sold both pieces to Colorado author Jerry Jenkins for $135,000, according to WTTW Chicago.The story is a striking example of how ordinary places can hold extraordinary objects. Beaty was not an art dealer or a collector with a specialist’s eye, but a freelance photographer who enjoyed searching garage sales and flea markets for pieces of Americana. What he found that day would eventually reshape the market value of Sallman’s original work. Read more about this surprising incident, as per the report, here:A familiar image from childhoodSallman’s Head of Christ is one of the most recognisable religious images in the world. It has been reproduced more than a billion times on prayer cards, candles, stamps, and countless other items, shaping how generations of people have visualised Jesus Christ. Beaty remembered seeing a reproduction of the painting in a school classroom when he was a child. That memory helped him recognise the artworks immediately when he saw them inside the Salvation Army store in February 2016.“I walked in and couldn’t believe something like this would be in the Salvation Army,” Beaty told WTTW. He said he knew from across the room that the pieces were originals, though he did not yet understand how rare they were until he began researching them online.Two works, one artistThe pieces were not identical. One was an oil painting, believed to be one of only five such works Sallman created. The other was a chalk drawing, a different medium but connected to the same artist and the same iconic image. Each work measured roughly three feet wide and four feet high. At the time Beaty found them, both were priced at $125, a figure that now seems almost impossible given what they would later sell for.Beaty negotiated the price down to $100 per piece. With tax, he paid $220 for both artworks, a purchase that would become one of the most remarkable thrift store finds in recent memory.Experts confirmed the valueAfter finding the pieces, Beaty sought expert confirmation of what he had. Sallman expert Leroy Carlson appraised the oil painting at $100,000 and the chalk drawing at $35,000, bringing the combined value to $135,000.That appraisal was significant because no original Warner Sallman work had previously been sold, according to Beaty. Many people told him the pieces would be difficult to sell without an art broker or auction house, and some doubted whether they were worth the appraised amount.Beaty spent the next two years trying to find a buyer. He contacted art brokers and museums, but nothing came together until a relative of Jerry Jenkins saw a Chicago Tonight segment about the discovery on Facebook and reached out.A buyer with a personal connectionJerry Jenkins, a Christian novelist and biographer best known for the Left Behind series, had a long-standing connection to Sallman’s work. He said he had felt drawn to the artist’s paintings since childhood, and later learned that his wife’s grandfather had known Sallman personally.That connection made the purchase feel personal rather than purely financial. Jenkins said it seemed like destiny that he and Beaty felt such a strong connection to the story and to the paintings.Jenkins has written more than 180 books, including profiles of Chicago Bears legends Walter Payton and Mike Singletary. He has also served on the board of the Chicago-based Moody Bible Institute for nearly two decades, giving him both the means and the context to appreciate the significance of the works.The $135,000 dealJenkins purchased both pieces for exactly the appraised value, $100,000 for the oil painting and $35,000 for the chalk drawing. The deal was finalised in a contract signed inside Beaty’s Chicago home earlier in March 2018.For Beaty, the sale was more than a financial win. It validated the instinct that told him the artworks were special, even when others doubted their value. “This sets the value of what an original Warner Sallman is worth now,” he said.The oil painting was believed to have hung for years inside Salvation Army buildings in Minneapolis and Des Plaines before Beaty found it. Jenkins planned to display it in a building next to his home where he does his writing.What happens to the chalk drawingJenkins said he was considering donating the chalk drawing in the future, either to a Christian institution or possibly back to the Salvation Army. That possibility adds another layer to the story, suggesting the artwork may eventually return to a public or religious setting.The oil painting, meanwhile, was set to travel to Colorado with Jenkins’ son the following week. Jenkins expressed excitement about having the works in his possession and gratitude that they had found a new home.The sale also highlights how art markets can be unpredictable. An object with no prior sales record can be difficult to price, but once a buyer with both interest and means steps forward, the market can establish a new benchmark almost overnight.A lesson in paying attentionBeaty’s story is often told as a thrift store miracle, but it is also a lesson in curiosity and persistence. He noticed something unusual, trusted his instincts, researched what he had found, and spent two years finding the right buyer rather than accepting a low offer.Not every thrift store purchase will turn into a six-figure sale. But the case shows why it can be worth looking closely at old paintings, signed prints, vintage photographs, and other items that may seem ordinary at first glance.For Beaty, the $220 purchase became a life-changing discovery. For Jenkins, it was a chance to own a piece of religious and artistic history connected to his own family story. And for the wider art world, it set a new reference point for the value of an original Warner Sallman work.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Congo Ebola outbreak claims nearly half of infected as cases cross 11,000
articles.summary: Six months after an Ebola outbreak was declared in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), the disease continues to spread, with more than 11,000 cases
articles.body: Six months after an Ebola outbreak was declared in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), the disease continues to spread, with more than 11,000 cases recorded and nearly half of those infected dying, according to government data.The outbreak is the deadliest among the 17 recorded in Congo and is on track to exceed the death toll of the West African Ebola epidemic, which killed around 11,000 people between 2014 and 2016.Efforts to contain the virus have struggled, with basic public health measures such as contact tracing and isolation remaining inadequate. Experts cited by the news agency Associated Press (AP) said there was little chance of bringing the outbreak under control within the next year.By the time the outbreak was officially announced in mid-May, 43 deaths had already been recorded, indicating that the virus had been circulating undetected for an extended period. It has since spread to eight of Congo's 26 provinces, with new hotspots continuing to emerge and putting further pressure on an already strained healthcare system.Gaps in surveillance and response fundingCommunity transmission remains high, with 80% of new Ebola cases being detected outside health surveillance systems, according to the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC). This means most infections have not been identified through official monitoring.Around one-third of deaths occur at home or elsewhere in communities, where burials and other procedures often take place without specialist supervision, increasing the risk of further transmission.The response has also been affected by repeated strikes by health workers over months of unpaid salaries. These stoppages have at times left patients with confirmed infections without treatment.Concerns have also been raised about the management of funds allocated to the response.Last month, the Africa CDC questioned the status of more than $700 million in Ebola aid that remains unaccounted for.Humanitarian organisation Doctors Without Borders, also known by its French acronym MSF, said there was a gap between the resources mobilised and the assistance reaching people affected by the outbreak.“A troubling disconnect between the considerable resources mobilised for the response and what is actually reaching patients, frontline workers, and communities continues,” the organisation said.Children account for a significant share of deathsChildren have been particularly vulnerable to the outbreak, especially those with pre-existing conditions such as malnutrition.Experts have said that most children affected by Ebola have not received specialised care, contributing to high death rates.According to Unicef data, children accounted for 35% of deaths recorded through November 4. Those under the age of five represented 21% of all deaths, while nearly 72% of infected children in that age group died.Conflict and attacks complicate containment effortsHealth workers have faced additional challenges in implementing prevention and containment measures, which sometimes conflict with local social and cultural practices.Since the outbreak began, health workers have been attacked, with some killed. Health facilities have also come under attack, further complicating efforts to respond to the disease.The outbreak has been concentrated in eastern Congo, particularly in Ituri and North Kivu, regions already affected by armed conflict. Fighting between government forces and hundreds of rebel groups, including the Rwanda-backed M23, has contributed to a severe humanitarian crisis.The Allied Democratic Forces, an Islamic State-affiliated rebel group, has also continued to attack civilians in the region.The spread of Ebola has raised concerns about transmission beyond Congo. Nigeria, Kenya and Uganda have confirmed cases, making the current outbreak the most geographically widespread Ebola outbreak on record.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: The French Republic’s forgotten promise of equality
articles.summary: French youth learn in school about the Revolution’s values but they do not see them reflected in their own reality.
articles.body:
Liberté, égalité, fraternité (liberty, equality, fraternity). Every French child learns the motto long before learning what it means to live up to it. It is a powerful promise. So is France’s habit of breaking it.

France has spent more than two centuries struggling to fulfil the French Republic’s founding principles of equality, liberty and fraternity. All citizens are supposed to be equal before the law, and public institutions are meant to serve the common good, regardless of origin or social background.

So, when students at under-resourced schools in Parisian suburbs or rural areas protest against missing teachers, deteriorating conditions in school buildings and years of neglect, their grievances extend beyond the classroom. They are challenging a system that promises equal opportunity while leaving many young people to pursue it with fewer resources than others.

As the movement attracted support from workers, unions and other protesters, it has become part of a broader confrontation over the cost of living, the dismantlement of public services and the state’s retreat from its social responsibilities.

The constitutional promise is explicit. The 1789 Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen establishes equality in rights, while the Preamble to the 1946 French Constitution makes public education at every level a duty of the state.

A republic cannot indefinitely tolerate schools whose quality depends on where children live and what their families can afford. When equality exists in constitutional texts but recedes from everyday life, the state loses credibility as the guarantor of l’intérêt general (general interest).

There is a historical reason this contradiction carries particular weight in France. The Revolution of 1789 challenged a social order in which privilege was attached to birth. The Third Estate, encompassing the vast majority of the population, carried much of the country’s economic burden while the nobility and clergy enjoyed advantages denied to ordinary people. The French Revolution abolished the legal foundations of this system and established equal citizenship as a founding principle.

More than two centuries later, there is something of a déjà vu. The French government is not the Ancien Régime, and today’s students are not a new Third Estate. Yet the question that animated 1789 has never entirely disappeared: what does equality mean when opportunity remains so dependent on the circumstances into which someone is born?

Hereditary privilege has been abolished as a legal principle, but social privilege can reproduce itself through family wealth, geography, access to good schools and professional networks. The mechanisms might have changed, but the problem has not disappeared.

This is what makes the school central to the current movement. Public schools form citizens; they should enable social mobility and should make merit more important than birth. When students protest because their schools lack teachers and adequate facilities, they are confronting the failure of an institution supposedly designed to make equality real. A system that tells young people their future depends on their effort cannot reasonably hold them responsible for failing to succeed in schools it has failed to equip.

While protest has deep roots in French history, it should not be reduced to a cultural stereotype. It is a recurring struggle over the authority of a centralised state that claims to represent the general interest. In May 1968 , student unrest expanded into a nationwide crisis involving millions of striking workers. The movement did not overthrow the state, but it demonstrated how a conflict within universities could expose wider questions about hierarchy, work and political authority.

In 2018, the Yellow Vests movement expressed a different, heterogeneous revolt against decisions perceived to impose disproportionate costs on ordinary households. These movements are not interchangeable. What connects them is the recurring demand that institutions justify their authority and honour their promises.

Today, while voicing their demands, student protesters have developed a distinct cultural language during protests. Anime, manga, memes and social media have become ways of expressing solidarity and defiance. References to One, Dragon Ball, the Avengers, Batman and other fictional worlds have also appeared in demonstrations, alongside creative slogans, costumes and visual jokes.

These types of symbols allow young demonstrators to recognise one another, communicate across schools and cities, and express a collective identity that does not depend on traditional political organisations.

However, their humour should not be mistaken for political shallowness. It is one way of making abstract ideas about injustice, freedom and solidarity tangible and visible both in France and beyond its borders.

Students’ legitimate grievances have met a state increasingly inclined to treat protests as a problem of security and to use violence as a response, rather than a warning about the condition of public institutions.

Security and public order have become an excuse for suppressing dissent. France’s experience after the 2015 terrorist attacks illustrates how exceptional powers can outlast the circumstances used to justify them: some measures associated with the state of emergency were incorporated into ordinary law in 2017. A government risks undermining its own legitimacy when it appears more capable of containing the consequences of institutional failure by force than of correcting them.

France keeps returning to its revolutionary ideals not because nothing has changed. It returns to them because their meaning remains contested.

The republic abolished privilege as a legal principle more than two centuries ago. It has yet to eliminate every way in which privilege reproduces itself. The students are forcing that unfinished question back into public life. And when they do, the state appears more capable of containing the consequences of its failures with brutality, rather than of repairing them. That is the contradiction at the heart of this movement, and the test it poses for the French Republic.

Many of the students in the streets will be among the voters in the April 2027 presidential elections. If history is any guide, the condescending response by Macron and his government will only harden student determination to participate in the election process. A higher youth turnout could benefit the left. However, it is up to the left to seize this opportunity, reconnect with younger generations and fill the political vacuum with a solid alternative.

articles.title: Norfolk residents join Hollywood stars in Parkinson's film
articles.summary: The movie, starring Laura Linney and Rhys Ifans, was filmed and set in Norfolk.
articles.body:
A woman living with Parkinson's said she was starstruck as she featured alongside Hollywood royalty in a new film based on the condition.

Sue Day was an extra in the movie Onwards and Sideways , which stars Laura Linney and Rhys Ifans, and was filmed and set in Norfolk.

Day, from Hindolveston near Fakenham and whose husband also has the condition, spoke of her nervousness at meeting the actors, but "very soon just developed a normal relationship with them".

She said she hoped the film would change people's perceptions and stereotypes of Parkinson's.

Written by the co-creator of Vicar of Dibley, Paul Mayhew-Archer, the film is based on his personal experiences over the past 15 years .

It follows Emma, played by Linney, and Ifans's Tony, as they navigate the five years after being diagnosed with Parkinson's on the same day.

Day, who starred alongside other Norfolk residents, said: "I think people think of Parkinson's as a disease where people just have the shakes, and there are so many different symptoms that you can have.

"For instance, my husband and I, we've got very different symptoms. Mine are quite physical... I find it difficult to walk very far. He, on the other hand, finds that he gets depressed in the mornings when he wakes up."

Tom Horne, who was also an extra, auditioned to be in the film after finding a flyer for it in a local Parkinson's group.

He said its authenticity was "absolutely perfect", including Ifans' portrayal of coming to terms with the condition.

He said: "I didn't know much about it until I got it. I just assumed it was some illness, nondescript, but it has about 40 different symptoms."

After driving him to the audition, Horne's wife Sheila was also given a part.

She said: "I really hope it's going to educate people on what Parkinson's is. So many people think it's just the shakes, but a lot of people with Parkinson's don't have a shake at all.

"We have made so many friends, because of the amount of people with Parkinson's and their carers that were in it."

Producer Hilary Bevan-Jones and director John Madden decided there was no better place than Norfolk to use as a backdrop.

The production was filmed in Fakenham, Blakeney and Morston, with Burnham Market Primary School transformed into the fictional Salt Marsh Primary.

Bevan-Jones said: "It was really important to us that we used as many local people as possible.

"[We] managed to find a lot of people living with Parkinson's in the local community and filmed a lot of beautiful dance classes at Binham Village Memorial Hall."

She said her father had Parkinson's and she hoped other people would connect with the movie.

"It's a very powerful film to work on," she said.

"The community were fabulous. Norfolk absolutely welcomed us with open arms."

Onwards and Sideways is out in cinemas and is being released on BBC One and iPlayer this Christmas.

articles.title: Israel: Making the Holy Land burn
articles.summary: For all its greenwashing, the Zionist state has ecologically devastated Palestine more than anyone else.
articles.body:
A month into this year’s olive harvest season, Israeli settlers and soldiers have already damaged or uprooted 4,500 olive trees in the occupied West Bank. Since January, they have destroyed 100,000 olive trees. In Gaza, since October 2023, 97 percent of Gaza’s two million olive oil trees have been wiped out. Between 1967, when Israel occupied Gaza and the West Bank, and the 2010s, it had destroyed more than 800,000.

I think of the devastating sight of uprooted trees in my grandfather’s olive grove every time I hear news of Israel sending yet another delegation to a climate, biodiversity, or desertification conference to boast of its “unique expertise” in “making the desert bloom” – a myth it has long propagated.

The destruction of olive trees is just one aspect of Israel’s broader war on the Palestinian land, from its vegetation and soil to its water and ecosystems. Since the Nakba of 1948, Israeli colonial policies have extended beyond land seizure and the displacement of its inhabitants to reshaping the natural landscape, undermining its capacity to sustain those who have lived on and cultivated it for generations.

In other words, contrary to its greenwashing claims, Israel made a blooming Palestine burn.

When the first Zionist settlers started coming to Palestine in the late 19th century, what they found was “a desert” that was already blooming. Palestinian land was producing not only enough food to feed its people but also to export to neighbouring regions within the Ottoman Empire and even across the Mediterranean to Europe.

Palestinians were growing wheat, barley and oats and harvesting olive and fruit trees. Closer to the Mediterranean coast, lush gardens produced various vegetables and fruit. In the more arid Naqab desert in the south, Bedouin tribes tended to herds of sheep, goats and camels, producing meat, milk and wool.

Palestinians co-existed with the various ecosystems they occupied: from wetlands to the dry desert. They tended to the land using techniques that reflected local conditions rather than seeking to engineer them. Local drought-resistant crops were grown in drier areas and more irrigation-dependent ones in valleys closer to water sources.

By contrast, Zionist settlers coming from Europe sought to reshape Palestine’s landscape to what was familiar to them. They planted trees imported from Europe, such as the stone pine, in some cases uprooting native species, including olive trees. They drained swamps, rerouted streams and tried to afforest desert landscapes.

Some of these activities had disastrous consequences for local ecosystems, including the introduction of non-native plants such as the eucalyptus, which burns easily and which has contributed to a higher frequency and intensity of wildfires.

Israel’s efforts to reshape the natural landscape were driven by the desire to erase Palestinian presence. Trees were planted over the remains of pillaged Palestinian villages to cover them up. Imported European-style agriculture wiped out native Palestinian techniques that had produced food for centuries.

The Zionist assault on the Palestinian land did not stop at the 1948 boundaries. As soon as the Israeli army occupied the West Bank and Gaza, it put under martial rule not just the people but also their natural resources.

Water has been at the centre of this process. As illegal settlements spread in the occupied territories, settlers started taking over local water resources. Today, Israel’s national water company, Mekorot, is responsible for running an extensive water system that reroutes water from Palestinian towns and villages to the Israeli settlements. It often cuts off water to Palestinians in the summer to ensure a steady supply to the illegal settlers.

This water theft has devastated Palestinian agriculture and ecosystems.

Meanwhile, land theft has featured not only violence against the Palestinian people but also against their soil. For years, the Israeli army and settlers have sprayed Palestinian land with pesticides to discourage farmers from working their fields. Meanwhile, burning and uprooting of trees and other vegetation, as well as settler construction, have damaged the soil and led to erosion.

In Gaza, ecocide has been taken to the extreme. The genocidal war unleashed on the Gaza Strip has devastated agricultural land, trees, soil and water.

These harms are compounded by bombardment and bulldozing. Israel has destroyed approximately 85 percent of buildings in the Gaza Strip, leaving an estimated 70 million tonnes of rubble containing various toxins. Israeli bombardment has dispersed heavy metals, including lead, cadmium, arsenic, tungsten and aluminium, as well as explosive compounds such as TNT, RDX and perchlorates.

These substances seep into the soil and groundwater, causing environmental damage whose effects may persist for years.

Meanwhile, the continuing bulldozing of buildings and land has stripped away the topsoil, which is rich in organic matter and nutrients essential for plant growth, further degrading agricultural land.

The paradox here is that the Israelis who claim to have an ancient right to the land are the very same people who damage and destroy it. This is highly surprising.

A coloniser sees land as something to capture, possess and exploit. The colonial relationship to land is one of abuse for the sake of material benefit. It is not care. It is not stewardship. It is not belonging.

The Israeli approach to Palestinian land – poison and destroy in order to control – contrasts sharply with the Palestinian one. Since 1948, Palestinians have faced constant attacks, destruction, theft of resources, pillaging. And yet, they have sought to rebuild, replant and rework over and over again.

My own grandfather, Hamdan, is an example of this Palestinian spirit. For four decades he looked over an eight-dunam olive grove that produced 1,500kg of olive oil each season.

During the 2008 war, the Israeli army bulldozed the grove. My grandfather did not relent. He replanted olive trees with my help. Just as the grove was beginning to recover, the Israeli army destroyed it again during the 2014 war.

For my grandfather, the olive trees were more than a livelihood. He saw them as his children, the fruit of years of care and his family’s bond to the land. Less than a week after their destruction in 2014, my grandfather died from the shock.

We did not relent either. My family set out to restore and replant the land with olive trees in 2015, which took several months. The trees then took three years to bear fruit. We managed to harvest olives for two seasons before the Israeli army bombed the grove during the 2021 war.

The land was so damaged that it was no longer suitable for olive cultivation. Clearing the contamination and burying the bomb craters took a long time, but we still managed to plant some of the land with seasonal crops like wheat. Then in December 2023, the Israeli army devastated the grove again.

I would be replanting that land again today if it didn’t lie beyond the ever-expanding “Yellow Line”.

That drive to tend to land is so deeply ingrained in Palestinians that even in the camps for the displaced, people are keeping small gardens in front of their tents, planting mint, basil and flowers.

Despite all the propaganda and greenwashing Israel deploys, it is increasingly clear to the world who can make the Holy Land bloom. It is not those who destroy, poison and bulldoze. It is those who are deeply rooted, who plant, grow and care. Those are the true owners of the land.

articles.title: Shane MacGowan: Tribute album gave mourning wife purpose
articles.summary: Three years after her husband's death, Victoria Mary Clarke's idea to put together a tribute album for her late husband came to fruition.
articles.body:
On the day of Shane MacGowan's funeral , his heartbroken wife found comfort in the same thing that moved and captivated the rest of the world that afternoon - the music that filled a parish church in Nenagh, County Tipperary.

Mundy and Camille O'Sullivan performed Haunted. Nick Cave sang A Rainy Night in Soho. And Glen Hansard and Lisa O'Neil led mourners in a send-off rendition of Fairytale of New York .

"I thought, well, if we just got all the people who were at the funeral on a record, that'd be something pretty special," Victoria Mary Clarke told BBC News NI.

On Friday, three years after her husband's death, that idea came to fruition with the release of 20th Century Paddy.

"It must be wonderful for Shane... I think up in heaven, he's very aware of what's going on," said Clarke.

There are 36 tracks on the new album - all penned by MacGowan - and 40 bands and soloists.

Among those are contributions from two acclaimed Irish artists who have passed away since recording their covers for the album.

Glen Hansard is featured performing Bottle of Smoke, while Moya Brennan provides her interpretation of Mother Mo Chroi.

"I feel love and connection between the artists (on the album) and Shane.

"And also, you know, for me personally, it feels like a lot of love because when somebody sends something nice to Shane, they're sending it to me."

The Pogues frontman died aged 65 at his Dublin home in 2023, following a hospital stay after being diagnosed with encephalitis.

Victoria was too fair to say who delivered her favourite cover on the album, but she was frank about how she personally benefited from the project.

"It gave me so much pleasure and it gave me so much joy and hope for the future to work on it because it gave me something to do every single day for three years and it got me out of bed and it got me to make new friends."

In the aftermath of her husband's death, that "social life and a sense of purpose" was invaluable to her.

But while the album is certainly bound up with MacGowan's death, it's not overshadowed by it.

"I think the artwork, if I had to pick, might be my favourite thing about the album," she chirped, an artist herself.

'Global respect as lyric writer and poet'

The term a 'who's who' doesn't quite capture the calibre and genre-defying diversity of the line-up featured on 20th Century Paddy.

There are hall-of-famers like Bruce Springsteen and Tom Waits.

Iconic, generation-crossing indie bands like The Jesus and Mary Chain and The Libertines.

And for anyone who needs reminding of how far above its weight Ireland punches when it comes to music, have a look at the back of 20th Century Paddy.

U2, Hozier and Bob Geldof - people with permanent residencies at top of the music industry.

There are stalwarts and custodians of the Irish folk tradition, Damien Dempsey perhaps foremost among them.

And lots of other artists, less established but very much in their ascendancy - Amble, Kingfishr and Madra Salach, to name but a few.

David Keenan, a singer-songwriter from Dundalk, whose thoughtful lyrics and intense live performances are invoke something of MacGowan himself, told BBC News NI he was honoured to be asked to add to the album.

"Fairytale of New York is as old as Christmas for me," said David.

But his epiphany moment came when an uncle gave him The Pogues' third album.

At 11 years old, Keenan said If I Should Fall from Grace with God "lit a flame" inside him.

"Up 'til that point it was just chart music.

"That (album) was the first time I heard all these references to mythology and drink and rebellion and, you know, heartache.

The Louth man described it like an awakening.

"It gave me permission as a kid to get stuck into real lyric writing. And to do it in the traditional and folk form."

On 20th Century Paddy, Keenan covered Sick Bed of Cúchulainn - a celtic punk ballad from their 1985 album Rum Sodomy and the Lash, the central allusion of which is the mythical Irish warrior Cúchulainn.

This has real significance for Keenan, who as a child in Louth, used to play near the standing stone (Clochafarmore) where Cuchulainn was said to have been killed.

He did his recording of the song in Drumlish, County Longford, where he said "Shane used to record too".

"It was just was surreal and at the same time perfect, you know."

Before putting his version down on tape, Keenan did something few artists would have done: he recited a poem he had written in Irish asking permission from MacGowan to sing the song.

"I felt connected to Shane's energy during the recording, you know."

Keenan said the quality of the artists on 20th Century Paddy showed the "global respect that was there for Shane's abilities, you know, as a lyric writer, a poet".

He added that, at a time when there is "a lot of pressure on young musicians now to go viral on TikTok and dumb themselves down... here's an artist who didn't do that".

"In an age of ChatGPT and generative AI", said Keenan, MacGowan is a reminder for "human beings to be authentic".

Keenan's top picks from the album included Summer in Siam covered by Tom Waits, Jimmy Artache's version of USA, Glenn Hansard's Bottle of Smoke and Steve Earle's If I Should Fall From Grace With God.

But, given the quality on the album, the list, he said, could have gone on... and on... and on.

articles.title: Visitors urged to take part in Owlman of Mawnan exhibition
articles.summary: An art installation inspired by an enduring piece of Cornish folklore opens.
articles.body:
A new exhibition has been inspired by an enduring piece of folklore.

Myths of the Owl Creature is a digital exhibition at Falmouth Art Gallery based on the Owlman of Mawnan, a legendary half man, half bird creature reported to have been seen flying in the village's woods and churchyard.

Artists Tom Milnes, Jess Pemberton and musician Seamouse are set to continue to develop the interactive installation throughout its three-week run, with exhibition attendees invited to join in the creative process.

Donna Westlake, of Falmouth Art Gallery, said: "Participation is at the heart of this project: visitors aren't simply observing the work, they're helping to make it."

At the centre of the exhibition is an interactive game world, (What's The Story) Mawnan Glory?, in which players take control of the owl being and roam the parish.

Visitors will have opportunities to contribute to the developing exhibition through workshops and events exploring drawing, collage, digital technology and creative storytelling.

According to Elizabeth Dale, a writer of local history, the first reported sighting of the half man, half bird was featured in the Cornish Echo newspaper in 1926.

Two boys who were in Mawnan woods said they had been attacked by "an enormous bird".

The next reported sighting was in 1976 when two girls camping in the woods said they had seen a huge bird "with red eyes and claws like a blacksmith's pinchers" flying around the church tower.

In 1995 a marine biologist from Chicago told the Western Morning News he had seen a "monstrous birdman" who had "looked like a vision of hell" near the church.

The exhibition is due to close on 28 November with an evening of interactive displays, live music and performances.

"Rather than presenting a finished artwork, Myths of the Owl Creature invites people to get involved, experiment and contribute to something that will evolve over time," Westlake added.

articles.title: Preston dancer wants to keep classical Indian dance alive
articles.summary: Sruthy Mahima Sanalkumar is nurturing the next generation of dancers at her dance school in Preston.
articles.body:
A dancer who opened a school in Preston says she wants to help keep traditional Indian classical dance alive in the UK.

Sruthy Mahima Sanalkumar, 28, grew up in Kerala, South India, and began training aged nine in the classical dance styles Bharatanatyam, Mohiniyattam and Kuchipudi.

After moving to Lancashire four years ago to study, she continued performing and established the Omkaram School of Dance.

She said audiences had embraced the performances and she hoped to introduce more people to the art forms.

Sanalkumar set up the dance school because she wanted to make a difference "to students who couldn't afford expensive dance schools".

She recently performed at Preston's Diwali celebrations in the Flag Market alongside other acts, including Preston-based Swati Dance Company.

She said the dance styles were closely linked to Indian culture, mythology and Hindu traditions, while also offering benefits for fitness, posture and wellbeing.

She said she still has the same passion for the "great traditions" and wants to spread her message of the joy of the dance forms to a wider audience, both through her performances and nurturing the next generation through teaching.

Sanalkumar recently performed in Preston Diwali celebrations at the Flag Market.

"It was fabulous," she said. "My aim is to bring it to wider audiences to love and embrace our traditional culture art forms," she added.

articles.title: What you need to know about Lincolnshire's 'out ER' signs
articles.summary: A total of 13 emergency evacuation routes were devised following the 2013 Boston floods.
articles.body:
Ever driven past an 'out ER' sign in Lincolnshire and wondered what it means?

One might assume they point motorists in the direction of a hospital or other medical facility.

However, they actually mark safe evacuation routes in the event of extreme events such as flooding.

Chief Fire Officer Mark Baxter, who also chairs the Lincolnshire Resilience Forum, said: "This is just one tool in our armoury to be able to support the evacuations of large amounts of people."

A total of 13 routes were devised across the county in 2015, two years after the Boston floods , states the Local Democracy Reporting Service.

The signs guide people to safer, higher ground and away from potential danger.

Baxter said: "These [routes] were designed and developed purely on the backdrop of our flood risk.

"We want our residents to understand why they are there and what they could be used for if we ever needed to enact them."

In Lincoln, the BBC spoken with Stephen Hill and Susan Ottaway.

Hill, 61, thinks few will know the purpose of the signs.

He said: "I just don't think people know what it is. It's a lack of knowledge."

Hill also pointed out how little clarity the signs give to those following them.

"It doesn't tell you where it's taking you," he added.

Ottaway, 56, also believes greater awareness is needed.

"It needs to be part of your driving exam," she said.

But she added: "You've got all the people who've already done their test who won't know what it is so you need some education on that."

articles.title: 'AI cameras could tackle widespread culture of dangerous driving behaviours'
articles.summary: The technology could be widely rolled out after nearly 19,000 offences were spotted in two weeks.
articles.body:
An artificial intelligence trial which uncovered nearly 19,000 potential driving offences in two weeks has highlighted a "huge problem" with driving behaviours in the West Midlands, said the region's first road safety commissioner.

AI-powered cameras installed outside Ladywood fire station in Birmingham and Fallings Park in Wolverhampton, captured drivers holding mobile phones at the wheel and failing to wear seatbelts. One image appeared to capture someone drinking from a wine bottle at the wheel.

Mat MacDonald said another image which showed a child "sitting unrestrained on a front passenger's lap," was "particularly shocking".

He said the findings pointed to a "widespread culture" of dangerous driving behaviours.

"What this trial has shown to me more than anything else, is we have a huge problem with these potentially lethal behaviours behind the wheel," he said.

The AI cameras have been "trained to recognise certain patterns", such as drivers who appear to be using mobile phones

Speaking about images that were captured during the two-week trial, which took place in March, MacDonald said he was not surprised by the number of drivers that were captured using mobile phones.

"I was equally disturbed, but not entirely surprised by numbers around mobile phones, specifically," he said.

"I travel by foot a lot and it is is almost impossible to get as far as the end of your street without seeing someone who is dialling and driving."

He said the cameras had also captured other concerning examples, including people appearing to inhale from balloons while driving.

"There was one particularly galling photo of someone drinking from a bottle of wine."

Simon Foster, West Midlands police and crime commissioner previously said the findings of the trial were "deeply concerning".

"We are closely evaluating these trial results to consider how this advanced AI technology can be deployed for future police enforcement," he said.

Road safety data from 2025 showed mobile phone use was linked to 32 deaths on UK roads while unfastened seatbelts were linked to 133 deaths, the WMCA said.

MacDonald, former chairman of campaign group Better Streets for Birmingham and an NHS doctor, said he was hopeful of the potential to roll the AI cameras out more widely in the future.

"I am working very hard to see what we can do to make this technology a reality on the roads in the West Midlands," he told the BBC.

"Hopefully this is the first step towards something that will enable us to start getting a grip of these types of behaviours, which... can end lives and ruin people's futures."

MacDonald said the trial was actually stopped earlier than planned because of how many possible road offences were being detected.

The technology identified 11,045 potential seatbelt offences and 1,163 potential mobile phone offences at Ladywood, and 6,030 potential seatbelt offences and 757 potential mobile phone offences at Fallings Park.

No enforcement was planned as a result of the trial, which was funded by the West Midlands Combined Authority (WMCA) working with the police and fire service.

He said he was keen to ensure the technology became more than just an "interesting experiment" and believed it had the potential to help change driver behaviour if rolled out more widely.

"We're currently in talks about what that looks like in terms of what resourcing we need to create to make this technology viable on our roads," he explained.

The road safety commissioner added: "Ultimately, we don't want to fine anyone. Ultimately, we want the number of fines and activations on these cameras to be zero because then we know we've done our job."

Dr Christophe Bastien, associate professor of Transport Safety at Coventry University said the technology offered an objective way of understanding how motorists behaved on the roads.

"The fact that 19,000 offences were identified during a relatively limited deployment suggests that actually, risky behaviour such as mobile phone use and seatbelt non-compliance, remain more common than many people think," he said.

He said the technology could help to improve road safety and target action in the future.

"These cameras provide an objective way to measure behaviour," he said.

"I think they are a way to target intervention where they most need it."

Dr Bastien, who has more than 25 years of experience in transport safety, added AI systems were not always perfect but could be used to support existing enforcement methods, rather than replacing them.

"I think in some respects, you still need the police to make the call," he said.

"The idea is not to punish people. It is the way people drive."

articles.title: Four Swordsmen: How China is reshaping its fighter jet fleet with J-35A stealth aircraft
articles.summary: China has expanded its frontline fighter aircraft concept from the traditional 'three swordsmen' to a new 'four swordsmen' formation, adding its J-35A
articles.body: China has expanded its frontline fighter aircraft concept from the traditional 'three swordsmen' to a new 'four swordsmen' formation, adding its J-35A stealth fighter to a lineup that includes the J-20, J-16 and J-10C. The development marks another step in the modernisation of the People's Liberation Army Air Force (PLAAF).The J-35A made its public debut at the Zhuhai Airshow on November 12, 2024. With its induction, China has become the second country after the US to develop and operate two fifth-generation stealth fighter aircraft. The US currently operates the F-22 Raptor and F-35 Lightning II. The J-35A, a medium-sized stealth fighter, has also drawn comparisons with the American F-35 because of its broadly similar design.According to a report by The Eurasian Times, Chinese military commentators and state broadcaster CCTV have increasingly presented the four aircraft as an integrated combat formation rather than separate platforms. The shift comes as China continues to expand its military aviation capabilities and prepares for the next generation of aerial warfare.What each fighter bringsFor years, the J-20 heavy stealth fighter, J-16 multirole fighter and J-10C lighter multirole aircraft were collectively described by Chinese military analysts as the PLAAF's 'three swordsmen'.The three aircraft were designed to complement one another. The J-20 provides stealth and advanced situational awareness, while the J-16 and J-10C contribute additional firepower and multirole capabilities.In a November 2022 interview with CCTV, J-16 pilot Zhang Yang explained how the aircraft worked together, with the J-20's situational awareness capabilities guiding the other two fighters, while the J-16 and J-10C delivered their firepower.The addition of the J-35A expands this approach by bringing another fifth-generation stealth platform into the formation. Chinese state media used the second anniversary of its public debut to highlight improvements in avionics, situational awareness and weapons integration. The aircraft could also eventually receive the full version of China's domestically developed WS-19 turbofan engine, although its development remains ongoing.The J-16, meanwhile, continues to provide substantial firepower. A recently reported configuration, described by Chinese defence experts as 'Beast Mode', showed the aircraft carrying eight PL-15 beyond-visual-range air-to-air missiles and two PL-10 short-range missiles.The PL-15 is designed for long-range aerial engagements, with an estimated range of around 200km, while the PL-10 is intended for close-range combat. The J-16's large weapons payload and advanced sensors make it an important component of China's aerial combat capabilities.Why China's fighter strategy is evolvingThe four-swordsmen concept reflects a broader shift towards network-centric warfare, in which stealth fighters, multirole aircraft and other military platforms operate as an integrated system.The J-20 and J-35A bring stealth and advanced sensing capabilities, while the J-16 and J-10C provide additional weapons capacity and operational flexibility. Advanced data links could allow the aircraft to share battlefield information and coordinate their actions.This approach is also relevant to the growing competition over sixth-generation fighter technology. The US is pursuing its Next Generation Air Dominance (NGAD) programme, centred on the F-47, while China has attracted attention with the development of aircraft identified as the J-36 and J-50.Future combat aircraft are expected to incorporate artificial intelligence, advanced electronic warfare, greater stealth and the ability to operate alongside unmanned combat drones.

articles.title: Iran has 1,500-2,500 missiles despite US claims of ‘decimated’ arsenal: Report
articles.summary: Iran may have between 1,500 and 2,500 missiles left in its arsenal, according to a US intelligence assessment.
articles.body: Iran may have between 1,500 and 2,500 missiles left in its arsenal, according to a US intelligence assessment. That suggests Tehran still has substantial capacity to strike American and allied forces if full-scale war resumes.US officials told the Wall Street Journal the estimate carries uncertainty, since it is hard to track how many missiles are launch-ready and how many sit in storage. Even so, they said Iran retains a formidable stockpile.Although US and Israeli strikes damaged Iran's missile-production facilities, Tehran has continued rebuilding its arsenal, largely using stockpiled components. However, the process has been slower than before the war, officials said.Iran also retains a large number of drones and short-range missiles.According to WSJ, the assessment contrasts with statements by US administration officials, including President Donald Trump, that Iran's military capabilities had been decimated. It has also featured in internal discussions within the Trump administration about whether to resume strikes alongside Israel, US officials said.Israeli military officials similarly estimate that Iran has more than 1,500 ballistic missiles, although assessments vary across the region because of the difficulty of determining the exact size of its stockpile.Simone Ledeen, who served as deputy assistant secretary of defence for the Middle East during Trump's first term, told WSJ that even the lower estimate of 1,500 missiles would mean Iran had replenished more than half of its estimated pre-war stockpile. She said Tehran had fully rebuilt its arsenal between the 12-day war in June 2025 and the start of the current conflict in February.Smarter tactics, wider reachIran has continued using ballistic missiles, drones and improved tactics to inflict damage on US military installations, radar systems and early-warning facilities across the Middle East. As a result, several US military assets have been moved to Israel, which is considered safer, Israeli and US officials said.Iran has reportedly also improved the effectiveness of its attacks by upgrading intelligence and targeting data, including with assistance from allies such as Russia, and combining missiles and drones in its operations.“It's not just the size of that arsenal. It's how Iran uses it, and its commanders have learned a few tricks to be more effective,” said Bilal Saab, senior managing director of Washington-based geopolitical-risk firm Trends US.Jim Lamson, a visiting research fellow at King's College London and former CIA analyst specialising in the Iranian military, said estimating the size of Iran's arsenal was difficult because of Tehran's secrecy, the number of missile producers it relies on and uncertainty over how many missiles could be assembled from finished components stored underground.Pre-war estimates of Iran's stockpile were also unclear, he said.“Having done this work for the government, I know it can be extremely low confidence even with all the classified information,” Lamson said.In April, the WSJ reported that Iran retained thousands of short- and medium-range ballistic missiles that could be recovered from underground facilities. US and Israeli strikes had collapsed the entrances to some of these sites, but satellite imagery later showed Iran had regained access to several by digging them out. An Israeli official said missiles stored underground had likely survived intact.In September, the Journal reported that Iran had resumed ballistic missile production using finished components held in stockpiles.An Israeli military official said that despite suffering heavy damage, Iran was rebuilding its arsenal and preparing for another major round of fighting.You use AI every day. articles.title: A Norfolk woman received 20 saffron corms as a birthday gift in 1997 and harvested just a teaspoon; 12 years later, she turned the experiment into a specialist spice business reviving the region’s 400-year-old saffron trade
articles.summary: A birthday gift of 20 saffron corms in 1997 led Norfolk botanist Sally Francis to establish a specialist spice business, Norfolk Saffron, in 2009.
articles.body: A birthday gift of 20 saffron corms in 1997 led Norfolk botanist Sally Francis to establish a specialist spice business, Norfolk Saffron, in 2009. What began as a small experiment at her family's farm near Burnham Market produced just a teaspoon of saffron in its first harvest. As the plants multiplied, Francis began selling the surplus at a local market, where it received an enthusiastic response. She subsequently turned the family’s saffron-growing efforts into a commercial venture, producing ISO 3632 Category I saffron and reviving a crop with a long history in Norfolk.How a birthday saffron plant grew into a business in NorfolkFrancis's interest in growing saffron began in 1997, when she asked her parents for a saffron plant for her birthday. She planted it at the family's smallholding near Burnham Market, on the north coast of Norfolk. Her initial harvest produced just a teaspoon of saffron.The company's official website provides further details about the beginning of the venture, stating that Francis's mother, Jill, bought her 20 saffron corms as a birthday present. The plants multiplied over the years, and the family gradually began producing more saffron than they could use themselves. Francis initially shared the harvest with family and friends before taking the surplus to a local market in 2009.How rural development funding helped Norfolk Saffron expand its productionThe response to the saffron sold at the local market encouraged Francis to explore commercial production. By 2009, the family had accumulated enough saffron to establish Norfolk Saffron as a business. According to the company's official account, Francis combined her knowledge of alternative crops with the farming experience of her late father, Edward, to develop the venture.The business was also supported by funding from the Rural Development Programme for England (RDPE), delivered through the Norfolk Coast and Broads Local Action Group. Norfolk Saffron subsequently developed into a commercial producer based at the family's smallholding, which has been in their possession since 1934. The company describes itself as England's leading commercial saffron producer.How Francis discovered Norfolk's 400-year history of saffron productionFrancis's research into saffron cultivation revealed that Norfolk had a history of producing the spice. National Geographic Traveller reported that around 400 years ago, the United Kingdom was an important saffron-producing region. Burnham Overy Staithe, a seaside port visible from the family's field, had previously been used to export locally grown saffron to the Low Countries.The discovery revealed a historical connection between the region and a crop that is now more commonly associated with countries such as Iran, India, Spain and Greece. According to National Geographic, Francis was surprised to discover that she had inadvertently helped revive a long-established local industry. The company also highlights the history of saffron exports from north Norfolk ports and describes its production as bringing Norfolk-grown saffron back to the market.How Norfolk's dry climate helps the farm grow autumn-flowering saffronSaffron comes from the purple-flowered saffron crocus, which has a growing cycle that differs from many other plants. Rather than flowering in spring or summer, the crocus produces flowers during autumn and winter before becoming dormant in summer. At Norfolk Saffron, harvesting takes place between October and November and generally lasts around four to six weeks.In an interview with National Geographic Traveller, Francis explained that the farm attempts to recreate the growing conditions of Crete as closely as possible using the conditions available in Norfolk. She also identified the county's relatively dry climate as a factor in cultivation. Francis, who is a botanist, has not disclosed all the farming methods used by the business, describing some of them as commercially sensitive.Why Francis starts harvesting saffron flowers as early as 7 amThe harvesting process involves collecting the largest flower buds, particularly those close to opening. According to National Geographic Traveller, Francis begins gathering flowers as early as 7 am during the harvest season. She explained that morning harvesting is important for the quality of the finished saffron.After collecting the flowers, Francis removes the stigmas, the parts of the flower used to produce saffron threads. Her mother, Jill, and her friend Mary help with this process, which involves carefully separating the stigmas by hand. The collected material is then placed in a specially made dryer before being prepared as saffron threads.How Saffron achieves the highest ISO 3632 Category I quality ratingNorfolk Saffron states on its official website that its annual independent laboratory testing consistently confirms that its saffron meets ISO 3632 Category I, the highest international quality category for saffron. The company compares its product with premium Spanish saffron, including Mancha and Coupé grades, and Sargol-grade Iranian saffron.The business also highlights several features of its production, including the use of whole, intact saffron threads and saffron from the most recent harvest season. It attributes the characteristics of its product to its soil, coastal microclimate, harvesting practices and drying methods. The company also states that its saffron has zero air miles, is fully traceable and is produced in accordance with UK food hygiene regulations.How an 18th-century saffron brioche recipe inspired FrancisSaffron is used in a range of dishes, including paellas, risottos, soups and ice creams. Francis told National Geographic Traveller that one of her personal favourites is saffron brioche, which she prepares using an 18th-century recipe. The recipe also provides a use for the broken saffron threads left over from the harvest.Norfolk Saffron operates from a smallholding of less than two acres, which is not open to visitors. Instead, the business sells its saffron through its online shop, alongside other products such as saffron flour and liqueurs. The company has also received several awards, including Great Taste Awards in different years, and was selected by the UK Government as one of its 50 Food Stars, recognising innovative food and drink businesses.From a birthday present in 1997 to the establishment of a specialist spice business in 2009, Francis's venture has developed around saffron cultivation in a region with a historical connection to the crop. Norfolk Saffron continues to produce and sell locally grown saffron, drawing on the family's farming background and its experience in cultivating the spice.You use AI every day. articles.title: 'Law on our side': Karnataka minister's big remark amid Mekedatu Dam row with Tamil Nadu
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Karnataka minister Priyank Kharge on Sunday said the law was on the state's side in the ongoing dispute over the proposed Mekedatu dam project
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Karnataka minister Priyank Kharge on Sunday said the law was on the state's side in the ongoing dispute over the proposed Mekedatu dam project on the Cauvery river. Kharge went on to add that that both Karnataka and Tamil Nadu would have to abide by the Supreme Court's directions."The Tamil Nadu PCC president will make statements and do everything within his capacity to protect Tamil Nadu's interests. Similarly, the Karnataka PCC president, the Chief Minister and all of us are duty-bound to protect our state's interests," he said.He further added: "Irrespective of our individual views, the Supreme Court has given directions, and the law is on our side. Whatever happens, it is going to benefit both states. In fact, Mr Shivakumar had offered the Tamil Nadu Chief Minister an opportunity to have a dialogue on this... Everyone has to follow the law of the land".His remarks come amid a row over the project, with the BJP accusing the Congress of adopting different positions in Karnataka and Tamil Nadu. Senior BJP leader and Leader of the Opposition in the Karnataka Assembly, R Ashoka, on Sunday alleged that the Congress was using the state's water rights for political gains while its leaders in Tamil Nadu were opposing the project.Ashoka pointed to Tamil Nadu Congress Committee president B Manickam Tagore's description of the Mekedatu project as illegal and his appeal to chief minister C Joseph Vijay to take legal steps to prevent its implementation. He also cited Tamil Nadu Congress MP Jothimani's opposition to the project.Accusing the Congress of double standards, Ashoka said the party had earlier organised a Mekedatu padayatra in Karnataka under the slogan 'Our water, our right', but had remained silent over opposition from its leaders in Tamil Nadu."Padayatra in Karnataka, legal battle in Tamil Nadu! Slogans in support of Kannadigas in Karnataka, a fight against the rights of Kannadigas in Tamil Nadu! What should one call this double standard of the Congress?" he said in a post on X.On Saturday, Shivakumar had reiterated the Karnataka government's commitment to pursuing the Mekedatu balancing reservoir project, maintaining that the state had the right to build the dam while protecting Tamil Nadu's share of Cauvery water. He said Karnataka would seek the necessary clearances and proceed in accordance with the Supreme Court's directions.What is the Mekedatu project?The Mekedatu project is a proposed multi-purpose balancing reservoir across the Cauvery river near Kanakapura in Karnataka's Bengaluru South district. It is intended to meet Bengaluru's drinking water requirements and generate hydroelectric power.Tamil Nadu has consistently opposed the project, expressing concerns that its implementation could affect the state's share of Cauvery water.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Why is so little council-owned art out on display?
articles.summary: Freedom of information figures show north-east council display less than 15% of the art they own.
articles.body:
The majority of artworks owned by North East councils are not being displayed, with some authorities in the region exhibiting less than 10% of their collections, figures have revealed.

According to data obtained by the BBC through a freedom of information request, only 3% of the art owned by Newcastle City Council is currently on display, with South Tyneside and Redcar and Cleveland showing 8% each.

In Sunderland 11% is displayed and Durham is showing 12% of its collection. About 15% is on show in Stockton. North Tyneside and Gateshead are the only local authorities to show nearly half of their collections, at 45% and 47% respectively.

Experts say the figures are far from unusual, with factors including available space and conservation requirements playing a part in how much can be shown.

Don O'Meara, president of the Society of Antiquaries of Newcastle upon Tyne, said some of the materials might be too delicate to display.

"I think the image that pops into people's minds is the scene at the end of Raiders of the Lost Ark where you have this vast store and you've got the man pushing the boxed up item to disappear into this vast archive, but actually a lot of these items would be quite small," he said.

Curator Niall Hodson said it would be "physically impossible" to exhibit everything at once, with most museums and galleries, including in Sunderland, having a "large number" of artworks on paper or textiles.

They would "gradually fade" if they were exposed to light full time, he said, adding: "You need to have objects like that rotated carefully on display for maybe a few months every few years.

"Otherwise they they won't exist in 10, 20 or 50 years time."

The former Sunderland Lib Dem councillor added: "The job will always be one of making sure it's rotated and seen by appointment, not one of getting it all out on display at once."

North East Museums Newcastle, which manages museums and galleries in the city on behalf of the council, said displays were changed regularly and the permanent collection was rotated.

Artworks in storage were also used for educational and research purposes and many could be viewed online, they added.

O'Meara said rotating the items was not as straightforward as it might look.

Insurance, fire risk, light levels, floor vibrations, security and the mobility of objects all had to be considered, he said.

"It would be fantastic if work could be rotated and seen as widely as possible, but I would really emphasise that simply moving an object does come with a cost," he said.

Hodson said at present Sunderland did not have capacity to show more artworks until extra museum and gallery space was created.

"Having 11% of the collection on display is probably higher than most public galleries manage," he said, adding: "Usually, it's in single figures.

"It's a good number for Sunderland and actually for any council to have that sort of percentage of artwork on display."

Sunderland's cabinet member for culture, tourism and heritage Ciera Hudspith said the current redevelopment of the city's Museum and Winter Gardens was also a chance to increase access to collections and "involve more people in interpreting Sunderland's heritage".

The venue closed for a revamp at the end of August.

New galleries will be created as part of the refurbishment, which Hudspith said would allow more of the city's collections to be shown.

"Like many museums and galleries, only a proportion of our collections can ever be displayed at any one time due to the space available, conservation requirements and the need to ensure exhibits are presented in the best possible way," she said.

Hodson said public art collections were "more accessible than people think" and many artworks could be seen online or by appointment.

"That's actually probably how most things that people really want to see will get seen," he said.

O'Meara said it would be "great" to get more art out in the community and look at ways it could be displayed "not always in a gallery", for example digitally or through converting empty shops into temporary exhibition spots.

"Access isn't just about being on permanent public display," he said, adding he would urge people to join societies and attend archive open events to "see what's on in their local museum and just appreciate it is for everybody.

"These are for people to celebrate and enjoy."

articles.title: No people or animals hurt in barn fire, says Surrey attraction
articles.summary: Chobham Adventure Farm says its Christmas experience "has suffered damage" in Saturday's blaze.
articles.body:
A popular family attraction in Surrey has said no-one was injured and none of its animals were hurt in a barn fire on Saturday.

Firefighters were called to the blaze at Chobham Adventure Farm near Woking just after 19:40 GMT.

Just before midnight, the attraction said "luckily" all the larger animals that usually live in the barn had been moved earlier for the winter holidays, while the small animals were already in their winter enclosure.

The farm's Christmas Experience within the animal barn "seems to have suffered the most damage", it added.

"We are pleased to say that no-one was hurt," Chobham Adventure Farm wrote on Facebook.

It said it was currently assessing the full impact on the build preparations for its upcoming festive schedule.

The attraction said it would contact people who had already booked tickets for its Christmas Experience via email "as soon as we have a clear plan in place".

"Our absolute priority right now is the safety of our team, our animals and our guests, as well as working closely with the fire service and investigators to secure the area," it continued.

In an update just after 20:30, Surrey Fire and Rescue Service said six fire engines were in attendance .

It urged people to avoid the area and advised people living nearby to keep doors and windows closed.

Firefighters told the BBC on Sunday morning that the blaze had been brought under control and they had left the scene.

Chobham Adventure Farm later said while its Animal Barn remained closed, the indoor soft play, small animal handling area and outdoor play were open as normal.

It added: "A huge heartfelt thank you to the emergency services for their rapid response and to our staff and local community for the incredible support we've already received.

"We will share another update as soon as we know more."

articles.title: A New York woman won $2 million for pain and suffering after a car crash and spinal fusion surgery; on November 12, an appeals court ordered a new damages trial unless she accepts $1.35 million instead
articles.summary: A serious car accident can leave injuries that require major surgery and have lasting effects on a person's life.
articles.body: A serious car accident can leave injuries that require major surgery and have lasting effects on a person's life. In New York, a woman who underwent spinal fusion surgery after a collision was initially awarded $2 million for past pain and suffering by a jury. However, the New York Supreme Court, Appellate Division, First Department, has ruled that the amount was higher than what could be considered reasonable compensation and ordered a reduction or a new trial on damages.In a November 12, 2026 decision available on Justia, the appeals court modified the earlier ruling in Estela Larrea v. Sanitation Salvage Corp. et al. The judges vacated the $2 million award and gave Larrea 30 days after entry of the order to accept $1.35 million instead. If she does not agree, the case will return to court for a new trial limited to those damages. The appeals court otherwise upheld the lower court's decision.Woman underwent cervical spinal fusion surgery after accidentThe case concerned Estela Larrea, who was 60 years old when the appeals court considered her compensation. She underwent a C5-C6 anterior cervical discectomy and interbody fusion, a procedure involving the removal of a damaged disc in the neck and the fusion of the affected vertebrae. The surgery involved a titanium plate and a plastic cage incorporating cadaver bone, which was secured with screws. The extent of the procedure formed an important part of the court's assessment of the compensation awarded for her past pain and suffering.A jury had awarded Larrea $2 million for this category of damages. However, Sanitation Salvage Corp. and the other defendants challenged the outcome after the trial, seeking a new trial on damages. They argued that the trial court had improperly prevented their proposed biomechanical engineering expert from testifying. Alternatively, they asked the court to set aside the jury's award and order a new trial on past pain and suffering.Appeals court rejects challenge to expert testimonyThe defendants argued that their biomechanical expert should have been permitted to explain the mechanics of the accident and its connection to Larrea's injuries. The trial court had conducted a hearing under the Frye standard, which examines whether a scientific methodology is generally accepted in the relevant field. The First Department upheld the exclusion of the proposed expert. It found that the defendants had failed to establish that his personal injury-causation analysis was generally accepted in biomechanics.The judges also identified problems with the information used by the expert. He had relied on assumptions about the weights of the two vehicles that were not supported by the evidence. He was also unaware that the truck involved in the collision carried a large metal construction container and did not know its weight.Other details were missing from his analysis. The expert did not know Larrea's body position at the time of impact or the type of seatbelt and headrest fitted in her vehicle. He was also unaware of her testimony that her car had moved approximately nine feet forward despite her foot being on the brake.The court further noted that the expert had not known that tape visible in photographs of Larrea's vehicle had been placed there after the accident. The tape obstructed part of the damage shown in the photographs. The appeals judges concluded that the expert's opinion lacked sufficient evidentiary value.$2 million award reduced to $1.35 millionWhile the appeals court upheld the exclusion of the defence expert, it separately examined whether the jury's compensation was reasonable. It concluded that the $2 million award for past pain and suffering materially exceeded what would be considered reasonable compensation under New York law.In reaching that conclusion, the judges referred to earlier cases involving spinal injuries and fusion procedures. These included a 2019 decision in which $1 million was considered reasonable compensation for a 69-year-old plaintiff, as well as earlier cases involving spinal fusion surgery and awards of $900,000 and $400,000. The court therefore vacated the $2 million award and ordered a new trial on past pain and suffering unless Larrea agrees to accept $1.35 million within 30 days after entry of the order. If she does not, a new trial will take place on that part of the damages.The November 12 ruling does not overturn the jury's entire verdict or allow the defendants' biomechanical expert to testify. Instead, it addresses the specific amount awarded for past pain and suffering while leaving the other aspects of the lower court's decision intact.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient.
